content.p: In September 1943, after Italy left the war, German troops on the Greek island of Cephalonia fought the Italian division that had garrisoned it and then shot many of the men who surrendered. Several accounts put the dead at roughly 9,500 of the Italian soldiers on the island, among them thousands executed after they had laid down their arms and others who drowned when ships carrying prisoners were lost. In Italy it is remembered as the largest massacre of Italian soldiers of the Second World War.

Justice came late and thinly. A Nuremberg tribunal sentenced a German general to 12 years in 1948 for his part in the events. It then took until October 2013 for an Italian military court to convict one former German corporal, in his absence, of taking part in the shooting of at least 117 Italian officers. The prosecutor who brought that case called the 70-year delay a denial of justice.
content.h2: A garrison caught between two orders
content.p: The Acqui Division had been stationed on the Ionian islands since April 1941. By September 1943 its commander was General Antonio Gandin, who spoke German, had won an Iron Cross in Russia and was regarded as pro-German, according to Restelli Storia, a history page that follows the days one by one. Nearly 12,000 Italians were on Cephalonia, against about 1,800 Germans who had arrived in August.

When the Italian government announced its armistice with the Allies on 8 September, the orders reaching the island contradicted each other. A message from the Italian command in Athens told the garrison not to turn its weapons on the Germans unless attacked, and later told it to hand heavy weapons to them. Later still, a message from the Italian supreme command in the south told Gandin to treat German troops as enemies. Restelli Storia says the last of these reached Cephalonia only on 13 September, a delay it calls a mystery. Meanwhile Gandin had been stalling the German commander on the island, Lieutenant Colonel Johannes Barge, who wanted the weapons handed over.

Gandin consulted the island's seven military chaplains, who advised surrender, and then, according to the same account, put three options to his men: fight alongside the Germans, give up their arms, or resist. Keep Talking Greece describes the same three choices. Restelli Storia says the answer that came back overnight was clear, that the troops wanted to fight, and that Gandin had by then settled on resistance too. A university student digital-history project likewise says a majority voted to resist. Restelli Storia also says that in the days before this, officers and men had been bitterly split, with some accusing Gandin of cowardice.

The Italians did not know that no relief was coming. Restelli Storia says the Allies lacked the forces for a landing on the island. German aircraft arrived, with around a hundred Stuka dive bombers and other bombers dropping some 32 tonnes of bombs, according to that page. The first day went reasonably for the Italians, who took many prisoners, but Gandin did not use the night to press forward. Barge was replaced by a new commander who brought in Edelweiss mountain troops, most of them South Tyroleans who spoke Italian. They had been told, the account says, that there should be no pity for "traitors", even the wounded.

Restelli Storia reports that messages from Hitler, relayed to the island, ordered first that officers who resisted be shot at once, and then that Italians who surrendered after fighting be shot as irregulars. It argues that the king had not yet declared war on Germany, which left the men legally without a flag. The Italians were outgunned: the page contrasts their old Model 91 muskets with German automatic weapons. Gandin wrote a note accepting surrender.

The killing began in the field. The Guardian reported on the wartime diary of a German corporal, Alfred Richter of the Edelweiss division, one of two German soldiers' diaries that came to light in Germany in March 2001. Richter described watching two Italian companies shot near Frangata with machine guns for about two hours, "without regard for rank or role, even the medics and the chaplains." On 23 September he noted executions in the harbour at Argostoli, in sight of Greek civilians, with the bodies left to rot.

One man who survived such a scene was Captain Amos Pampaloni. The Guardian reported that at Dilinata he surrendered with about 80 gunners. When he protested at being robbed of his wallet and watch, a German officer replied that the rules of war applied to prisoners, not to traitors, and shot him through the back of the neck. The rest of his men, wounded included, were killed with machine-gun fire. Pampaloni, who was 90 when the paper interviewed him, still bore the marks on his neck. He recalled that the mule handlers were spared, "because every mule responds best to his own master", and that the German soldiers left ten minutes after the shooting, singing. He then spent a year with the Greek resistance on the mainland.

The surviving Italian officers were shot at a place called the Casetta Rossa, Italian for little red house. Il Fatto Quotidiano, reporting the 2013 trial, says 129 officers are said to have been killed there by two firing squads, with seven more killed the next day in reprisal. One squad was commanded by a lieutenant named Otmar Muhlhauser. Restelli Storia says the priest Don Formato witnessed the killings and that 37 officers survived thanks to his intervention, shouting for it to stop. The same page says Lanz later told Nuremberg that Gandin had been tried and condemned as an irregular, and adds its own view that Gandin was probably shot at the Casetta Rossa.

Not all the dead were shot. Keep Talking Greece says about 3,000 men drowned when a ship carrying prisoners towards camps in the Reich sank. Restelli Storia puts the first such loss at 800 prisoners bound for Patras on a ship that struck a mine, with almost all dying, and two more ships lost in October and December and 1,360 more dead. Around 1,000 men stayed on the island, according to the same page, and 3,000 to 4,000 were sent to camps. It says that on 11 November 1,250 prisoners rejoined the Italian side.

The totals differ from source to source. Keep Talking Greece counts 1,300 dead in combat, 5,155 shot after capture and 3,000 drowned over eight days. The Guardian says 9,500 of a garrison of 11,000 died and that 5,000 are believed to have been executed. Restelli Storia gives roughly 1,300 Italian and 300 German dead in the fighting and about 5,000 executed, but also cites an author it writes as "Screiber", who counted 6,500 shot and 1,350 to 1,400 drowned. The student project says 9,500 were killed or taken prisoner. The sources do not agree. Keep Talking Greece adds that about 200 bodies had been thrown down a well and were only recovered and sent home a few months before the Italian president's visit in 2001.

The Cephalonia killings reached a courtroom first at Nuremberg. The Hostage Case, Case 7 of the Subsequent Nuremberg Proceedings, tried German military defendants on charges that included the murder of civilians in Greece, Yugoslavia and Albania. The trial opened before Military Tribunal V on 15 July 1947. Among its charges was drafting orders that denied surrendering enemy troops quarter or the rights of prisoners of war. The tribunal gave judgment on 19 February 1948, finding eight defendants guilty of at least one count and acquitting two. The Holocaust Memorial Museum's account does not say which of the charges concerned Cephalonia, but Il Fatto Quotidiano and Restelli Storia agree that General Lanz received a 12-year sentence.

Both also say he served only part of it: Il Fatto, quoting the prosecutor De Paolis, says three years; Restelli Storia says five. Restelli Storia adds that the indictment against Lanz concerned the shooting of Gandin and his staff, that the court knew nothing of the 5,000 shot or of the killings on Corfu, and that it accepted that, thanks to Lanz, only the senior officers had been executed.

The book by De Paolis and Insolvibile lists criminal files on the Cephalonia killings opened in the military prosecutor's office in Rome between 1950 and 1960, and the cover of one file found at Palazzo Cesi in 1994. Restelli Storia gives its own account of those years. A parent's complaint in 1952 named German soldiers and also about thirty Italian officers accused of provoking the revolt. In 1957 a military prosecutor sent 30 Germans and 27 Cephalonia survivors to trial. A few months later an investigating judge cleared all the Italians, and 21 of the 30 Germans were also spared, the page says, after intervention by two government ministers. The other nine never appeared, and the inquiry closed in 1960.

In Germany, according to that page, the Dortmund prosecutors shelved an investigation in 1969 because it leaned on a book containing invented characters, and reopened it in 2001, looking at seven former Wehrmacht officers. Munich prosecutors then dropped the case against Muhlhauser. The date differs: the De Paolis volume lists a Munich decision of 27 July 2006, Keep Talking Greece says a German court cleared him in 2006, and Restelli Storia says September 2007, on the ground that the offence was ordinary murder rather than a war crime. Rome opened a new file against him on 2 January 2009, after a complaint from two Italian women who had lost their father on the island. He died on 1 July 2009 at the age of 89, while a hearing was pending.

By then the Rome prosecutor had a second name. Marco De Paolis said in March 2012 that Alfred Stork, a former Wehrmacht corporal, should be tried for the execution of at least 117 Italian officers. Keep Talking Greece, quoting ANSA, said the evidence included an alleged confession he had made to German prosecutors in 2005 that he belonged to one of the two firing squads. According to Il Fatto Quotidiano, he said he had been told they had to shoot Italians who were considered traitors, and that his squad, under "a lieutenant", fired from dawn to afternoon and left 73 officers dead.

The case was hard. Il Fatto reported that Stork never repeated his statement and that no one could be found to identify him as a member of the squad. A carabinieri non-commissioned officer who worked on the investigation told a hearing that a comrade shown an old photograph of Stork with other soldiers recognised all of them except Stork. De Paolis relied on a German expert report and several witness statements, and called the silence of the units involved a wall of omertà. He also rejected the argument that orders had to be obeyed on pain of death, saying soldiers had refused at Cephalonia and no punishment of those who refused was on record.

On 18 October 2013 the military tribunal in Rome sentenced Stork, in his absence, to life imprisonment for taking part in the shooting of at least 117 Italian officers. He lives in Germany. De Paolis said it was the first conviction for the events on Cephalonia since Nuremberg, and that the court appeared to have accepted that a criminal order is no shield. The partisans' association ANPI said the verdict recognised for the first time the guilt of German soldiers responsible for the killings, and recognised its own right to damages. The size of compensation was left to a civil court. The same page notes that the shooting took place on 24 September, though the opening line gives 27 September.

Restelli Storia says that in 2010 the Rome court also began proceedings against two other 86-year-old former members of the 966th Fortress Grenadier Regiment, accused of killing 170 Italian soldiers who had surrendered. It says both men had denied guilt when questioned in 1965 and 1966, and again in Rome, and that investigations were continuing when it was written. The pages opened here do not report an outcome.

For decades the massacre was little discussed. The Guardian argued in 2001 that it had been all but erased from Italian remembrance because Cold War priorities discouraged recalling atrocities of the German army, as opposed to the SS, so as not to embarrass a pillar of western defence. The student project makes a similar claim and ties the renewed attention to Louis de Bernieres' novel Captain Corelli's Mandolin and its 2001 film.

The decision of the garrison not to give up its weapons is sometimes called the first act of the Italian resistance, the Guardian notes. Restelli Storia reports that Italian president Carlo Azeglio Ciampi visited Cephalonia on 1 March 2001 and used those words, and that Giorgio Napolitano marked the Liberation anniversary on the island on 25 April 2007, the first time a sitting president had celebrated that day abroad. The same page records that for Rochat the answer is both yes and no, and that Rusconi does not consider Cephalonia comparable with the later Resistance.
